speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me more about your skin lesions, such as when they appeared and if they are painful or itchy? Also, how long have you had the fever and wrist pain?

speaker: Patient
text: 17-year-old male. The patient presents with a 3-day history of pain in his left wrist, which worsened this morning accompanied by chills and malaise. He recounts having a self-resolving left knee pain the previous week. Reports recent return from a camping trip in Minnesota. Sexually active with one female partner. No history of trauma to the wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your recent trip to Minnesota and the history of migratory joint pain, have you noticed any circular, expanding rash on your body that might resemble a bullseye? Also, did you observe any ticks on your person or clothing during or after your camping trip?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain in the left wrist. I also have Chills, Malaise, Painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on both wrists and hands, Swelling and erythema of the left wrist, Severe tenderness to palpation and passive movement of the left wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: The painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the hands and wrists are highly characteristic of Secondary Syphilis, which can present with arthritis and systemic symptoms like fever. REQUEST TEST: RPR, Treponemal antibody test

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative syphilis tests and your recent trip to Minnesota strongly suggest Lyme disease, despite the atypical rash description. Let's confirm this with specific Lyme serology and check for signs of a tick bite or bull's-eye rash you might have missed. REQUEST TEST: Lyme Western Blot, CBC, ESR

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Complete Blood Count: WBC 15,000 /μL (elevated), Hemoglobin 14 g/dL, Platelets 300,000 /μL; Lyme Western Blot: Negative; ESR: Not provided in data

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative Lyme test and the specific description of painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the hands and wrists, combined with acute monoarticular arthritis, are classic signs of Erythema Multiforme, often triggered by an infection. I need to check for the most common infectious triggers, particularly Herpes Simplex Virus. REQUEST TEST: HSV PCR, Mycoplasma pneumoniae serology

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative HSV and Mycoplasma results, combined with the high white blood cell count and acute monoarticular arthritis, suggest a septic joint rather than a reactive process. Given the specific skin lesions and systemic symptoms, I need to rule out bacterial endocarditis or disseminated gonococcal infection. REQUEST TEST: Blood Cultures, Joint Aspiration for Gram stain and culture

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Blood Cultures: Pending at the time of examination; Joint Aspiration Left Wrist: WBC >50,000 /μL (markedly elevated), Gram Stain: Gram-negative diplococci seen

speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of Gram-negative diplococci in the joint fluid confirms a diagnosis of Disseminated Gonococcal Infection. DIAGNOSIS READY: Disseminated Gonococcal Infection
